proof:
# A shared-tilt theorem in an explicit normal cone for every simplex dimension

Let d>=2, T=conv(0,e_1,...,e_d), V=|T|, and
Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d. Let r_-N,...,r_N be nonnegative, nonzero,
symmetric and concave, with r_0=R>0. The fiber at base k is
r_k T; a zero radius denotes the singleton {0}. Set

    M=V sum_(k=-N)^N r_k^d,
    y=(0,R/(d+1),...,R/(d+1)).

In particular y belongs to the actual peak fiber. This note proves
an exact directional result for these fibers, retaining EVERY integer
tilt in the halfspace. It does not assert the full chain theorem
for arbitrary continuous normals, or general (OC).

Normalize a nonzero nonnegative continuous normal u by sum_j u_j=1.
Relabel the coordinates so that u_1=a is largest and let
b=max_(j>=2) u_j. Write t=1/(d+1) and q=2^(-1/d). Assume a>b and

    (a-t)/(a-b)<=q.                              (1)

Then for the through-point halfspaces

    H_beta={ (z,x): beta z+u.x>=Rt },

the minimizing shared tilt is beta=0. The exact minimum mass is

    inf_beta vol_MI(S intersect H_beta)
      = V C_u sum_k (r_k-Rt/a)_+^d,
    C_u=a^(d-1)/product_(j=2)^d (a-u_j)>=1.       (2)

No separate tilt has been introduced for different pairs.

## 1. Conditional simplex law proves all paired tilts at once

Condition (1) is understood with a>b. The explicit cone in Section 3
below guarantees this hypothesis. Since a>=1/d>t, its numerator
is positive. Because q<1, (1) implies b<t.

Write a uniform point of T as

    X_1=W,
    X_j=(1-W)Y_j,  j=2,...,d,

where Y is uniform on the standard (d-1)-simplex. The change of
variables has Jacobian (1-W)^(d-1). Since V_(d-1)=dV_d, W has
density d(1-W)^(d-1) on [0,1] and is independent of Y. Set
Z=sum_(j=2)^d u_j Y_j, so 0<=Z<=b. Then

    u.X=aW+(1-W)Z.

Conditioned on Z=z, the upper tail at threshold v is

    G_z(v)=1,                           v<=z;
           [(a-v)/(a-z)]^d,             z<=v<=a;
           0,                           v>=a.   (3)

Now consider a positive radius r<=R and set v=Rt/r>=t. Its
two reflected fibers have conditional thresholds v-s and v+s,
where s=|beta|k/r>=0 for the pair at bases +/-k. We show

    G_z(v-s)+G_z(v+s)>=2G_z(v)                    (4)

for EVERY s>=0 and every z in [0,b]. If v>=a the right side is
zero. Otherwise v>=t>b>=z, and (1) implies

    G_z(v)<= [(a-t)/(a-b)]^d<=1/2.               (5)

If v-s>=z, both tail terms in (4) are given by the convex function
(a-v)_+^d/(a-z)^d; its midpoint inequality proves (4). If v-s<z,
the first tail is 1 and (5) proves (4). This covers the equality
boundaries as well. Averaging over Z proves the unconditioned
pair bound. A zero-radius fiber contributes zero d-volume and
can simply be omitted.

Every pair realizes equality at the SAME original beta=0. The
own fiber k=0 has no beta dependence. Thus the total mass is
minimized at beta=0, exactly as asserted. This argument neither
assumes nor concludes that independent nonzero pair optimizers
can be matched by one tilt.

## 2. Exact cap volume and truncation consequence

Since b<t and r<=R, the zero-tilt cutting plane u.x=Rt is above
every vertex height other than that of r e_1. If ar<=Rt the cap
has volume zero. Otherwise it is the simplex at r e_1 cut by
that plane. Its edge fractions toward the other vertices are
(ar-Rt)/(ar), for the edge toward 0, and
(ar-Rt)/[r(a-u_j)] toward r e_j. The determinant volume formula
therefore gives its volume as

    V (ar-Rt)^d/[a product_(j=2)^d(a-u_j)].

The positive-part version covers ar<=Rt. Summing gives (2).
Each a-u_j lies in (0,a], which proves C_u>=1.

Apply the proved truncation theorem in
`candidate c3c2ca0e4dcbdc9d`
at p=d and c=Rt/a. It yields

    inf_beta vol_MI(S intersect H_beta)
      >= C_u (1-t/a)^(d+1) M
          + V C_u c(R-c)^d/[R(2N+1)].           (6)

This is a geometric use of the finite sequence theorem: (4)
first controls every oblique shared tilt, and only then is the
zero-tilt sum converted to a mass ratio. It does not substitute
an integral for the integer fibers.

## 3. An explicit nonempty cone that gives the desired chain constant

Define

    A_d=(q-t)/(2q-1),
    B_d=t/[1-(Gamma_d/2)^(1/(d+1))],
    a_d=max(A_d,B_d).                            (7)

Then 1/2<a_d<1. Thus the hypothesis a>=a_d describes a nonempty
closed cone of nonnegative normals around each coordinate normal,
with a nonempty relative interior. Every such normal satisfies (1)
and every closed ambient halfspace with that continuous normal
containing y has mass STRICTLY greater than

    (Gamma_d/2) M.                               (8)

Here is a verification of all constants. For integer d>=2 the
binomial formula gives (1+1/d)^d>2 (the first three terms suffice),
so Gamma_d<1/2 and q>d/(d+1)=1-t. In particular q>1/2.
One computes

    A_d-(1-t)=(1-q)(1-2t)/(2q-1)>0,

while A_d<1 is equivalent to q>1-t. Thus 1/2<A_d<1.
Also

    (1-t)^(d+1)=Gamma_d*d/(d+1)>Gamma_d/2,

so (Gamma_d/2)^(1/(d+1))<1-t and B_d<1. This proves the
claimed range of a_d.

If a>=A_d, then b<=1-a and

    (a-t)/(a-b)<=(a-t)/(2a-1)<=q.

The last rational function decreases with a on a>1/2, because
its derivative is (2t-1)/(2a-1)^2<0, and equals q at A_d.
Thus (1) holds. If also a>=B_d, then
(1-t/a)^(d+1)>=Gamma_d/2. Formula (6), C_u>=1, and the positive
remainder prove (8) for through-point halfspaces. A halfspace of
the same orientation containing y has a no larger threshold and
therefore contains its through-point counterpart. This proves
the claim for every such closed halfspace.

All nonvertical cutting hyperplanes in this proof have zero
d-dimensional volume in each positive fiber; singletons have
zero d-volume since d>=2. Closed boundary traces therefore obey
the exact formulas used above. Purely vertical halfspaces through
base 0 contain all of the own fiber and at least one complete
fiber from each reflected pair, hence at least M/2. They also
satisfy (8). None of these statements controls the remaining
continuous normal directions outside the displayed cone.

When N=0 the formulas still hold for the single actual fiber;
there are no paired terms or tilt issue. When N>=1, concave
linear interpolation of the radii yields a convex body with the
given fibers, even when an endpoint radius vanishes. The result
also applies after any invertible continuous affine change and
an affine translation of the common vertex depending on the
base, since these maps preserve the integer coordinate and
multiply all fiber volumes by one constant determinant.
